standard.title: Target language features similar to and different from English
standard.description: recognise that the target language has features that may be similar to or different from English
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have noticed sound patterns and tonal features of the target language (AC9LCH2U01) and recognised how language features construct meaning (AC9LCH2U02). They have compared some sound and writing features with English. They have not yet systematically compared structural features, word order, vocabulary borrowing, or grammatical categories across the two languages using beginning metalanguage.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise that the target language has features that are similar to and different from English — including word order, sound patterns, borrowed vocabulary, text features and basic grammatical categories — and can describe comparisons using simple language.

nodes.label: Word order and structural similarities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify where word order and sentence structure in the target language is similar to or different from English, with examples.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples where word order in the target language is the same as English and at least one where it differs, using a simple sentence example for each.
nodes.typical_width: Compare word order in statements, questions and phrases across the target language and English; notice where modifiers, numbers, and descriptive words appear relative to nouns; discuss where the two languages follow similar logic and where they diverge.
wider: Investigate a specific structural difference — for example, how dates, names or expressions of time are ordered differently — and explain the rule in simple terms
Compare equivalent phrases in bilingual texts and map the structural differences — annotate a short text to show where target language and English word order matches and where it diverges
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising structural similarities and differences is the foundation for language comparison. Students who assume the target language works exactly like English will make systematic errors and cannot develop the comparative metalinguistic awareness that this descriptor and the Y3-4 strand require.

response_modes.reason: Structural comparison requires students to hold two language systems in mind simultaneously. Explicit comparison frames — 'in English this goes here, in the target language it goes there, because...' — scaffold the reasoning before students can conduct comparisons independently.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two examples of word order similarity between the target language and English
Identifies at least one example of word order difference with a correct explanation

nodes.label: Vocabulary borrowing across languages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that languages borrow words from each other, and identify examples of borrowed words in the target language or English.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two borrowed words in the target language (from English or another language) or in English (from the target language), and explain what they mean.
nodes.typical_width: Explore borrowed vocabulary in the target language — words adopted from other languages; recognise that English also borrows from the target language and other languages; discuss why languages borrow words and what this reveals about cultural contact and influence.
wider: Research a set of borrowed words in the target language and trace their origin — identify what cultural or historical contact led to the borrowing
Compare borrowed words in the target language with borrowed words in Australian English — identify patterns in what gets borrowed (food, technology, fashion) and why

response_modes.reason: Vocabulary borrowing is best understood through varied examples across categories — food, technology, transport, popular culture. Exposure to multiple examples across domains builds the general insight about language contact before students can reason about why borrowing occurs.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Vocabulary borrowing is a concrete and often surprising entry point into the idea that languages influence each other. Background learners who know both languages often recognise borrowed words with delight. Width investment here builds an understanding of languages as living, interconnected systems rather than isolated codes.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two borrowed words and explains their meaning in context
Can explain in simple terms why languages borrow words from each other

nodes.label: Text features and metalanguage for language types
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in text features across the target language and English, and use simple metalanguage to describe word types.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two similarities or differences in text features between a target language and English text, and correctly use at least two metalanguage terms (e.g. verb, noun, adjective) to describe language features.
nodes.typical_width: Compare bilingual texts (picture books, songs, multimedia) and notice similarities and differences in punctuation, layout, and organisation; use simple metalanguage to describe word types in the target language and English; discuss grammatical categories that appear different across the two languages.
wider: Compare two bilingual versions of the same text (e.g. a folk tale in target language and English) — identify all the structural and textual differences and compile a class comparison list

Explore a grammatical category that works differently in the target language from English — for example, where English uses one word type and the target language uses a different structure — and explain the difference in simple terms

response_modes.reason: Text feature comparison and metalanguage use integrate structural comparison (node 1) and vocabulary knowledge (node 2) into a broader reading of how the two languages work as systems. The teaching investment is in making comparison explicit — naming what students notice — rather than leaving metalinguistic awareness implicit.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two text feature similarities or differences between a target language and English text
Correctly uses at least two metalanguage terms to describe language features
